title: Beta check-in: workload-aware batching defaults (existing customer)
summary: BrightLedger shared early results from enabling tiered batching defaults on two production routes. Standard tier reduced cost per 1M tokens ~18–22% on non-streaming summarization with p95 latency roughly flat. They hit an edge-case regression on a streaming chat route when switching to cost-efficient tier: elevated timeouts and worse first-token latency at high concurrency + long prompts, likely due to queue delay + KV cache pressure behavior. Customer also asked for clearer visibility into “effective config” when tier defaults apply vs explicit overrides.
topics: Observed $/token savings and GPU utilization changes
Streaming cadence / first token latency regression in cost-efficient tier
Timeout spike + cancellation behavior under concurrency
Need for effective config visibility and troubleshooting workflow
Next steps: trace IDs, rollback one route, Redwood to propose override knobs + confirm fix timeline
next_steps: BrightLedger to send 10–15 request IDs / trace IDs from the timeout window (include route, model, and whether streaming) to Redwood (Miguel).

Redwood (Sofia) to review queue-delay + decode prioritization settings for cost-efficient tier on streaming workloads and suggest a safe override (e.g., cap queue delay, adjust decode weight) for BrightLedger to test.
Redwood (Monica) to share SDK snippet showing how to set batching_tier per route and how explicit batching overrides interact with tiers; include link to docs draft when ready.
BrightLedger to revert the streaming chat route back to standard tier today; keep summarization route on standard tier for another week to gather more stable cost numbers.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up after Redwood reviews traces (target: week of Mar 17).
action_items: BrightLedger (Ryan): revert /chat streaming route to standard tier and confirm timeout rate returns to baseline (today).
BrightLedger (Emma): export trace/request IDs from 2025-03-11 18:00–22:00 UTC window and email to Miguel (by 2025-03-13).
Redwood (Sofia): analyze traces for queue delay + batch formation + KV cache pressure; propose override config + hypothesis (by 2025-03-14).
Redwood (Monica): send “tier vs explicit override” explainer + SDK examples (by 2025-03-14).
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: Mar 12, 2025
Time: 4:00 PM UTC
Duration: 41 min
Title: Beta check-in: workload-aware batching defaults (existing customer)
Attendees:
- Miguel Santos (Redwood) 
- Monica Patel (Redwood)
- Sofia Ivanova (Redwood)
- Emma Li (BrightLedger)
- Ryan Patel (BrightLedger)
- Sonia K. (BrightLedger)

Auto-generated (Fireflies)
Summary: Customer reported cost savings on standard tier, but saw timeouts on cost-efficient for streaming chat at high concurrency.
Action Items: (see above)

Transcript

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Hey everyone. Emma, Ryan, Sonia—good to see you again. Thanks for making time. Um, goal today is basically beta check-in on the tiered batching defaults. What you turned on, what broke, what got better. 

[00:14] Emma Li: Yep. Sounds good.

[00:16] Monica Patel: Hi all.

[00:17] Sofia Ivanova: Hey.

[00:20] Miguel Santos: Cool. Before we dive in—quick roll call on your side? 

[00:23] Sonia K.: Yeah, I’m Sonia, PM for our “assistant in the ledger” feature. I’m mostly here to understand if we can keep the cost savings without hurting user experience.

[00:32] Ryan Patel: Ryan, platform. I own the gateway and the Redwood integration bits. 

[00:36] Emma Li: Emma, ML. I’ve been looking at latency charts and some of the output diffs.

[00:41] Miguel Santos: Great. Sofia is our runtime scheduling lead, Monica is SDK/docs. I’m customer success.

[00:48] Miguel Santos: So maybe start with what you enabled. Ryan, can you recap which routes are on which tier?

[00:55] Ryan Patel: Sure. We did two routes. 
- Route A is non-streaming summarization, like batch jobs but it’s still online. That one we set to “standard”. 
- Route B is our interactive chat, streaming, on the UI. We tried “cost-efficient” there for a day and then… we backed it out last night.

[01:15] Miguel Santos: Got it. And models?

[01:18] Ryan Patel: Both are on your… uh, “Llama 3.1 70B instruct” hosted. I might be butchering the name. It’s the 70B chat model.

[01:26] Sofia Ivanova: That’s fine, we know which one.

[01:29] Miguel Santos: Cool. Emma, what did you see on standard tier? Let’s do the positive first.

[01:34] Emma Li: Yeah. So standard tier for summarization was honestly pretty good. We compared against our previous config where we had explicit max batch size set, and a small queue delay. Standard tier dropped our cost per… per million tokens by about 20 percent. I think the range was 18 to 22 depending on the day.

[01:55] Miguel Santos: Nice.

[01:56] Emma Li: And p95 latency stayed about the same. It moved a bit but within noise, like maybe plus 3 percent one day, minus 2 percent the next. GPU utilization went up though. Our dashboard in your Console, the utilization graph looked healthier, like less spiky.

[02:12] Sofia Ivanova: Do you know what your concurrency looks like for that summarization route?

[02:16] Ryan Patel: It’s bursty. During business hours it’s like 20 to 50 concurrent. End of month it spikes to maybe 120 for a bit. But typical is 30-ish.

[02:26] Sofia Ivanova: And prompt lengths?

[02:28] Emma Li: Mostly medium. We feed in, like, customer transaction context. Prompt around 1.5k to 3k tokens, output 200 to 400. Some outliers at like 8k prompt.

[02:41] Sofia Ivanova: That’s super helpful.

[02:44] Miguel Santos: So for standard tier the takeaway is: savings without latency pain. Sonia, anything from user side?

[02:52] Sonia K.: No complaints on that workflow, it’s behind the scenes. We just care that the job finishes. So the savings are great.

[03:00] Miguel Santos: Great. Now the other route—cost-efficient + streaming. What happened?

[03:06] Ryan Patel: Uh, yeah. We enabled cost-efficient tier around Monday midday. At first it looked fine. Then during our afternoon peak yesterday we got a bunch of timeouts. Our overall timeout rate went from basically 0.05% to like 0.6% on that route.

[03:25] Emma Li: And first-token latency got noticeably worse for some users. Like it wasn’t “slow generation” exactly, it was that the stream took longer to start. People saw the typing indicator and nothing came for a couple seconds.

[03:37] Miguel Santos: Do you have numbers?

[03:39] Emma Li: Baseline p95 time-to-first-token on standard was about 1.4 seconds. With cost-efficient it jumped to 2.3-ish. p99 got ugly, like 6 to 8 seconds, and then some requests just hit our client timeout at 10 seconds.

[03:56] Sofia Ivanova: Was the token cadence after first token stable? Like once it started streaming was it okay?

[04:02] Emma Li: Mostly yes. Once it started, it felt normal. Maybe slightly more “bursty” like a few tokens then pause then more tokens, but that could be perception.

[04:12] Ryan Patel: We also saw increased cancellations. We have users who abandon the chat if it doesn’t start quickly.

[04:18] Miguel Santos: Ok. That lines up with what we worry about on streaming. Cost-efficient tier tends to allow more queueing to form batches.

[04:26] Sofia Ivanova: Yeah. In cost-efficient, the max queue delay is higher, and also the scheduler tries harder to batch prefill. That can be bad for time-to-first-token.

[04:36] Emma Li: Right. The thing is we expected a tradeoff but not the timeouts.

[04:41] Miguel Santos: Yeah, timeouts are not expected. Did anything else change? Traffic shape, prompt size, tools, function calling?

[04:48] Ryan Patel: Uh, we did roll out a feature on Tuesday morning: we started including more conversation history. So the prompt got longer. Not crazy but it moved from maybe 800 tokens average to like 2k average.

[05:02] Emma Li: And we also turned on tool calling for a subset. It’s basically, the model decides to call “lookup_invoice” which hits our backend.

[05:10] Sofia Ivanova: That’s big. Tool calls change the sequence of decode and can add pauses and additional requests.

[05:16] Emma Li: Yeah, but the timeouts were happening before tools. Like in the initial response.

[05:20] Sofia Ivanova: Understood.

[05:22] Miguel Santos: When you say timeouts, is it your client timeout, or are you seeing 5xx from us?

[05:27] Ryan Patel: Both. Mostly client-side. But we saw some 524-ish and a few 429. Not sure if that was rate limit or backpressure.

[05:36] Sofia Ivanova: 524 sounds like upstream timeout. 429 could be admission control.

[05:42] Ryan Patel: Yeah. 

[05:44] Miguel Santos: Did you capture request IDs?

[05:47] Ryan Patel: We have some, yes. I can pull a sample. 

[05:50] Miguel Santos: Please do. It’ll help us correlate with queue delay metrics and batch formation.

[05:56] Emma Li: Our suspicion is it started batching too aggressively, and then with the longer prompts the prefill phase is heavy, so it’s waiting to form a batch and then the prefill takes longer and… you’re already close to timeout.

[06:11] Sofia Ivanova: That’s a good hypothesis.

[06:13] Miguel Santos: Sofia, do we have any known edge cases similar?

[06:17] Sofia Ivanova: We’ve seen streaming regressions when queue delay is set for cost and the workload shifts to longer prompts. Also KV cache pressure can trigger extra work—compaction or eviction—and that can add tail latency. It’s more likely under high concurrency.

[06:32] Emma Li: Yeah, concurrency was high. It was like 200 concurrent streams at peak. 

[06:36] Sofia Ivanova: 200 streaming is pretty intense. 

[06:39] Ryan Patel: It’s not constant, but yeah, we had a marketing email go out, so everyone clicked.

[06:45] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[06:47] Sonia K.: From a product standpoint, we can’t have that. If chat doesn’t respond, users assume it’s broken.

[06:53] Miguel Santos: Totally.

[06:55] Monica Patel: Can I ask—were you relying on any explicit batching overrides before, or was it default behavior?

[07:00] Ryan Patel: Before this beta, we had an explicit config. We set max_batch to 8 and queue delay to 3 milliseconds. Something like that. Then with tiers, we removed those and just set batching_tier.

[07:12] Monica Patel: Okay, that’s important. We’ve been hearing confusion about precedence. The intended behavior is: explicit overrides win. But if you removed them, you’re fully on the tier defaults.

[07:23] Ryan Patel: Right. But it’s not super obvious what the effective config is after you pick a tier. Like we want to confirm what queue delay actually became.

[07:32] Miguel Santos: Yeah, we’ve got an “explain effective config” endpoint coming, but not GA yet. Today it’s more… indirect via docs.

[07:40] Emma Li: That would help a lot. Because we’re trying to debug and it’s like, okay, is it queue delay? Is it max batch? Is it decode priority? Hard to know.

[07:51] Sofia Ivanova: For streaming cost-efficient, the default queue delay is higher than you were using. That alone can move TTFT.

[07:59] Ryan Patel: That makes sense.

[08:01] Miguel Santos: Let’s talk about cost impact on that chat route—did you see savings before you rolled back?

[08:07] Emma Li: Some, but not as clean. We saw maybe 10 to 12 percent token cost reduction. But because of timeouts and retries, the “effective” cost might be worse.

[08:18] Ryan Patel: Also, users re-ask the question when it times out. That’s extra tokens.

[08:23] Miguel Santos: Right.

[08:24] Sofia Ivanova: And streaming cost savings usually come with a bigger risk. Standard tier is usually the recommended baseline for streaming.

[08:31] Sonia K.: Wait, so is cost-efficient basically not meant for streaming?

[08:36] Sofia Ivanova: It can be used, but it’s more sensitive. We’re adding guardrails. For some workloads, we’ll likely clamp queue delay for streaming even in cost-efficient.

[08:46] Miguel Santos: That’s part of why we’re doing this beta.

[08:49] Emma Li: Can I mention one more weird thing?

[08:51] Miguel Santos: Please.

[08:52] Emma Li: We saw a small quality difference. Not like hallucinations, but sometimes the first chunk of the stream started mid-sentence? Like it didn’t begin with a capital letter. It was rare. Might just be sampling randomness though.

[09:06] Sofia Ivanova: Hmm. That can happen if the client is stitching partials weirdly, but also if there’s any cancellation/resume behavior. Are you doing any proxy buffering?

[09:15] Ryan Patel: We’re using nginx in front. We try not to buffer streams but… there’s settings. I’ll double check.

[09:22] Monica Patel: Also if there are retries, sometimes the UI might show partial from the first attempt and then continue from the second. I’ve seen that.

[09:30] Emma Li: That might be it. We do a retry on 524.

[09:34] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[09:36] Miguel Santos: Okay, so immediate mitigation—sounds like you already rolled back the streaming route?

[09:41] Ryan Patel: We set it back to standard at midnight UTC. We’re waiting to see today’s peak.

[09:47] Miguel Santos: Good.

[09:48] Sofia Ivanova: For your use case, I’d recommend standard for streaming, and then if you want to squeeze costs, do explicit overrides in a controlled way—like small queue delay increase, but keep decode priority high.

[10:01] Emma Li: That’s what we want: a safe baseline, then tweak.

[10:05] Monica Patel: On that note, how did you set tier? Per-request header? Or config at the route level?

[10:11] Ryan Patel: Route-level in our Redwood config. For now it’s static.

[10:15] Monica Patel: Great.

[10:17] Miguel Santos: Let’s dig into the regression window. Ryan, do you remember roughly when it spiked?

[10:23] Ryan Patel: March 11, around 6 PM to 10 PM UTC was the worst.

[10:29] Miguel Santos: Perfect. If you can send us 10 to 15 request IDs from that window, we can pull internal traces.

[10:36] Ryan Patel: Yep.

[10:38] Sofia Ivanova: Also, if you can include prompt length buckets or at least “short/medium/long” per request, that helps.

[10:45] Emma Li: We can add prompt token count from our side, yeah.

[10:49] Miguel Santos: Great.

[10:51] Sonia K.: Can I ask: is this something you expect to fix before GA? Because we do want cost-efficient if it’s safe.

[10:59] Miguel Santos: Yes, the goal is safe-by-default. We don’t want cost-efficient to surprise-streaming users. We’re likely going to add guardrails: streaming clamp and overload integration so it sheds load instead of queueing forever.

[11:13] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly.

[11:14] Ryan Patel: Shedding load sounds scary too.

[11:17] Sofia Ivanova: It’s better than timeouts, because you get a fast 429 with a reason code and you can degrade gracefully, like switch tier or fall back model.

[11:26] Emma Li: Yeah, at least it’s deterministic.

[11:29] Miguel Santos: We can also talk about fallback policies. Are you using any fallback today?

[11:34] Ryan Patel: Not automatically. We thought about falling back to a smaller model for chat but we haven’t done it.

[11:41] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[11:43] Emma Li: Another thing: on cost-efficient we saw the “queue delay” metric in your Console go up. It was like… I don’t remember exact. Maybe median 8 ms but tail at 80 ms.

[11:56] Sofia Ivanova: 80 ms queue delay is not crazy, but combined with long prefill it compounds.

[12:03] Emma Li: Exactly. And then there’s network and our nginx. So it adds up.

[12:09] Monica Patel: This is where the effective config would help. Because “cost-efficient” implies bigger delay but how much bigger depends on model family and streaming.

[12:19] Ryan Patel: Yeah. Also we got confused about naming. Is it “cost-efficient” with a dash, or “cost_efficient” underscore? In config it’s underscore.

[12:28] Monica Patel: Yep, config is cost_efficient. Docs will show both but the literal value is underscore.

[12:35] Miguel Santos: Good catch.

[12:37] Miguel Santos: Let’s make sure we capture your ask: 1) keep standard tier as baseline for streaming, 2) provide clear knobs for controlled cost-saving, 3) provide visibility into effective config.

[12:49] Sonia K.: And 4) don’t break TTFT. That’s like the main user perception metric.

[12:55] Sofia Ivanova: Absolutely.

[12:57] Emma Li: We also care about p99. Some users are on slow networks.

[13:02] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[13:03] Sofia Ivanova: Can I ask what client timeout you have?

[13:06] Ryan Patel: For first byte we use 10 seconds. For overall completion it’s 60.

[13:12] Sofia Ivanova: Okay. So any TTFT >10 is a hard fail.

[13:16] Emma Li: Yeah.

[13:18] Sofia Ivanova: We should design cost-efficient streaming to keep p99 TTFT comfortably below that. Like <5 seconds ideally.

[13:28] Miguel Santos: Emma, did you see any OOMs or errors that suggest memory pressure?

[13:33] Emma Li: Not directly. But we did see a few responses with “server overloaded” messages. Not sure if that’s your error.

[13:40] Ryan Patel: Some were 503 with “over capacity.”

[13:45] Sofia Ivanova: That’s admission control. If cost-efficient allowed more queueing and then hit pressure, it might flip into overload mode, causing mixed behavior.

[13:55] Miguel Santos: Right.

[13:57] Monica Patel: For what it’s worth, we’ve had other customers compare to vLLM. vLLM tends to batch aggressively too, and they see similar TTFT tradeoffs unless tuned.

[14:07] Emma Li: Yeah, we tried vLLM internally. Good throughput, but we spent weeks tuning. That’s why we like the tier idea.

[14:15] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[14:17] Sonia K.: Quick question—if we keep chat on standard tier, can we still use cost-efficient for other routes? Like embeddings or rerank? 

[14:24] Miguel Santos: Yes. In fact, cost-efficient is usually great for non-streaming, high-volume routes like embeddings or batch summarization, as long as the queue delay doesn’t violate SLO.

[14:35] Ryan Patel: We don’t do embeddings with you yet, but maybe later.

[14:39] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[14:41] Miguel Santos: Can we talk about how you measured cost savings? Was it your internal $ estimate or our metering?

[14:48] Emma Li: We used your Console cost per token metric. And we also approximate based on usage because we have internal chargeback.

[14:56] Miguel Santos: And savings was 18-22% on standard for summarization.

[15:00] Emma Li: Yeah.

[15:01] Sofia Ivanova: That’s very consistent with better batching.

[15:05] Miguel Santos: Great. That’s a good outcome we can cite internally (anonymized).

[15:10] Sonia K.: As long as it’s anonymous, sure.

[15:12] Miguel Santos: Yup.

[15:14] Miguel Santos: Let’s dig deeper on the edge-case. Emma, you mentioned longer prompts and tool calling. Do you have a sense which dimension correlated more with timeouts? Was it long prompt requests timing out more?

[15:26] Emma Li: Yes. When we bucketed by prompt length, the >4k bucket had like 3x the timeout rate compared to <1k. Not a lot of samples but it was pretty clear.

[15:39] Sofia Ivanova: That suggests prefill batching is the culprit.

[15:42] Ryan Patel: Also, during that spike we had a lot of concurrent sessions. So it might be queue plus prefill.

[15:49] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly.

[15:51] Miguel Santos: Sofia, what’s a safe workaround we can propose without waiting for code changes?

[15:58] Sofia Ivanova: For streaming chat, keep tier = standard. If you still want cost reduction, you can set tier = standard and apply explicit override like slightly higher max_batch but keep max_queue_delay small. Also ensure decode priority remains high. Another approach is to route long-context requests to standard and short ones to cost-efficient, but that requires policy routing.

[16:20] Ryan Patel: We can do per-request routing but it’s a bit of work.

[16:24] Miguel Santos: Probably not in the next week.

[16:26] Monica Patel: For now, simplest is: streaming route standard, non-streaming standard or cost-efficient depending on SLO.

[16:34] Emma Li: Agreed.

[16:36] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[16:37] Sonia K.: What about the naming. Is “fast” tier something we should consider for chat to improve TTFT?

[16:44] Sofia Ivanova: Fast tier prioritizes latency. It tends to keep queue delay extremely low and it may under-batch. So cost goes up. For user-facing chat, fast can make sense, but you need to be okay with higher $ per token.

[16:57] Sonia K.: Probably not.

[16:59] Emma Li: Maybe for VIP users.

[17:02] Miguel Santos: That’s actually a common pattern.

[17:05] Ryan Patel: We also have dedicated capacity for some workloads. For chat we’re hosted right now. Does that change anything?

[17:12] Miguel Santos: On Dedicated, you get more predictable throughput, but the tier behavior is similar. The difference is you can provision capacity to avoid overload.

[17:21] Ryan Patel: Got it.

[17:22] Sofia Ivanova: And on Dedicated, if you’re at the edge of GPU memory, cost-efficient may push it harder, so we’d want to consider KV cache pressure settings.

[17:33] Emma Li: Makes sense.

[17:35] Miguel Santos: Let’s talk about visibility. You asked for effective config. If we can’t give the endpoint today, what would be acceptable? Headers? Console view? 

[17:45] Ryan Patel: Header would be great. Like “x-redwood-effective-queue-delay: 12ms” or something. Even if it’s not every knob.

[17:54] Monica Patel: We’re working on that. There’s an internal PR for an “explain config” API that Console can show. I can share a draft doc once we have it.

[18:04] Emma Li: That would help debugging.

[18:07] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[18:09] Miguel Santos: Any other feedback on standard tier? Anything surprising?

[18:14] Emma Li: One thing: we saw less variance. p50 stayed same, but the “mid tail” improved. That’s good. It means batching is more consistent.

[18:24] Sofia Ivanova: Great.

[18:25] Ryan Patel: Also, we didn’t have to touch anything. That’s the big win.

[18:31] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[18:33] Miguel Santos: On the regression, we’ll treat it seriously. If you send request IDs we’ll dig into our internal spans: queue delay histogram, batch size, prefill vs decode time.

[18:45] Ryan Patel: Okay.

[18:47] Emma Li: We can also send our own charts.

[18:50] Miguel Santos: That’d be helpful.

[18:52] Sonia K.: What’s the timeline for you to change cost-efficient streaming defaults? 

[18:58] Sofia Ivanova: Hard to promise, but near-term we can add a guardrail: if streaming=true, clamp queue delay to a lower bound even in cost-efficient. And we can adjust decode prioritization so TTFT is protected. That’s in flight.

[19:16] Miguel Santos: We’ll follow up after we see your traces.

[19:19] Ryan Patel: Ok.

[19:20] Emma Li: Another small thing: docs. The docs page we found didn’t say clearly that explicit overrides beat tier selection. We had to guess.

[19:30] Monica Patel: That’s a good callout. We’ll fix that. The intention is: if you set max_queue_delay_ms explicitly, we will not override it when tier is set. Tier is a default preset.

[19:42] Ryan Patel: Cool.

[19:44] Miguel Santos: Great. Anything else from your side?

[19:47] Emma Li: Not really. We’re happy with standard. We just want to avoid that streaming edge case.

[19:53] Sonia K.: Yeah, if you can make cost-efficient safe for streaming, we’d be interested later.

[19:59] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[20:01] Miguel Santos: Let’s recap next steps. Ryan, you’ll keep chat route on standard and confirm timeout rate returns to baseline today.

[20:09] Ryan Patel: Yep.

[20:10] Miguel Santos: Emma, you’ll export request IDs from the 6 to 10 PM UTC window yesterday and send them to me. Include prompt token counts if possible.

[20:19] Emma Li: Yes.

[20:20] Miguel Santos: Sofia will analyze on our side and propose a safe override if you want to try cost-efficient again in a controlled way.

[20:29] Sofia Ivanova: Yup.

[20:30] Miguel Santos: Monica will send an explainer about tier vs overrides, plus SDK snippet and naming (cost_efficient).

[20:37] Monica Patel: Yes.

[20:39] Miguel Santos: And we’ll schedule a follow-up next week.

[20:43] Sonia K.: Works.

[20:45] Miguel Santos: Great. Thanks everyone.

[20:47] Emma Li: Thanks.

[20:48] Ryan Patel: Thank you.

[20:49] Sofia Ivanova: Thanks.

[20:50] Monica Patel: Bye.
